info.desc: Paul's Boutique is the second studio album by American hip hop group Beastie Boys, released on July 25, 1989 on Capitol Records. Featuring production by the Dust Brothers, the recording sessions for the album took place at Mario G's Studio in Los Angeles and The Opium Den in Brooklyn, New York from 1988 to 1989, after which the recordings underwent mixing at the Manhattan-based Record Plant Studios. podcast.body: Released on July 25, 1989, this album was a significant departure from *Licensed to Ill*, lacking the "frat boy goofiness" and "big guitars" of its predecessor. Initially, sales were dismal, and Capitol Records stopped promotion after two singles, leading to the firing of the label's president and others. Despite its commercial failure at the time, the album was artistically and technically very advanced for its day, blowing away the rap and hip-hop community. The Beastie Boys, with production team The Dust Brothers, spent close to two years meticulously crafting it, sampling no fewer than 105 different songs, expertly woven into the fabric of each track. The band cleared all samples, paying approximately $250,000, which was considered reasonable at the time but would cost millions today due to subsequent sampling lawsuits. Today, it is recognized as an "absolute masterpiece" and a landmark album in hip-hop, sampling, producing, and recording engineering. "But we just didn't see it at the time, but this record was so advanced, both artistically and technically for its day, that we just didn't get it."

podcast.body: Released on July 25, 1989, this second album by the Beastie Boys sought to embody their New York identity through its artwork. Ad-Rock was inspired by an old radio commercial for a Brooklyn men's clothing store named Paul's Boutique, which was no longer in business. To create the cover, a sign for "Paul's Boutique" was fabricated and hung over a store called Leigh Sportswear at the corner of Ludlow and Rivington streets on Manhattan's Lower East Side. Photographer Jeremy Chutan took a panoramic shot for the cover. Initially, the album was met with disappointment from fans expecting more frat boy anthems like those on their first album, and was branded a failure. However, it was later recognized as a landmark recording praised for its production, sampling, and clever use of beats, becoming an essential part of music collections. "When the album was released on July 25, 1989, the whole thing landed with a thud."

podcast.body: Released on July 25th, 1989, this album was a conscious effort by the Beastie Boys to create a highly creative rather than commercial record, avoiding being pigeonholed after "Licensed to Ill." Produced with The Dust Brothers over nearly two years, it meticulously sampled no fewer than 105 different songs, which were expertly woven into the tracks. Despite its artistic and technical advancement, it was a commercial disaster at the time, leading Capitol Records to stop promoting it after two singles and even resulting in the firing of the label's president. It cost the band about $250,000 to clear all the samples, a sum considered reasonable compared to today's costs. The album is now recognized as a masterpiece and a landmark in hip-hop, sampling, producing, and recording engineering. "Today we recognize Paul's boutique as an absolute masterpiece."

podcast.body: The Beastie Boys' 1989 album, *Paul's Boutique*, is notable for containing samples from 105 different songs. The band cleared all these samples, albeit under older rules, incurring nearly $300,000 in sample clearance costs, a sum that would be prohibitively expensive for such an album today. "In 1989, the Beastie Boys released their Paul's Buti Calbum, a recording containing samples of 105 different songs."

podcast.body: This album, released in 1989, was the highly anticipated follow-up to *Licensed to Ill*. It was initially a commercial flop because it diverged significantly from expectations, being ahead of its time. The packaging is noteworthy, best viewed in its vinyl gatefold form, which unfolds from 12x12 inches to 12 inches by three feet, revealing a panoramic photo of Ludlow Street on Manhattan's Lower East Side, specifically from the perspective of 99 Ludlow Street. While MCA's alias Nathaniel Hornblower was credited, the real photographer was Jeremy Chattan, the Beastie Boys' original bass player from their punk era, who took about 30 rolls of film, including some lost bird's-eye shots from 101 Park Avenue. "Instead, they released something so ahead of its time that the record was initially a commercial flop."
